title: Proximity-induced superconductivity in a bilayer graphene quantum point contact
authors: Clara Galante-Agero, Christoph Adam, Artem O. Denisov, Jonas D. Gerber, Markus Niese, Alexandra Mestre-Torà, Marta Perego, Jessica Richter, Takashi Taniguchi, Kenji Watanabe, Klaus Ensslin, Thomas Ihn
abstract: We report the realization of a gate-defined quantum point contact (QPC) in bilayer graphene proximitized by a single aluminum superconducting electrode. Superconducting correlations induced in the ballistic channel enhance the conductance plateaus beyond their normal-state values. In addition, we observe a pronounced above-gap conductance anomaly which serves as a spectroscopic signature of the loss of superconductivity and the associated collapse of the Andreev excess current. By reconstructing the nonlinear current-voltage characteristics, we find that the magnitude of the excess current increases as successive QPC modes are populated. Additionally, we find that the switching current associated with the loss of superconductivity follows the underlying mode structure of the QPC, exhibiting discrete levels consistent with a heat dissipation-driven transition. These results demonstrate that the one-dimensional transport modes of the QPC govern both the equilibrium proximity effect and the non-equilibrium dynamics of the hybrid system.
summary: The researchers studied superconductivity in a graphene QPC coupled to an aluminum superconductor. They demonstrated that the quantized one-dimensional electronic modes of the QPC dictate both the equilibrium proximity effect (enhanced conductance via Andreev reflection) and the non-equilibrium dynamics, evidenced by stepwise changes in the superconducting breakdown current.
main_problem: To investigate how quantized one-dimensional transport modes of a Quantum Point Contact (QPC) govern both the equilibrium proximity effect and the non-equilibrium dynamics in a hybrid superconducting/normal conductor system.
main_result: The excess supercurrent and the switching current associated with superconductivity loss both exhibit discrete, quantized steps that directly follow the opening of successive QPC transport modes.
method: Measurements include linear conductance ($G$) vs. gate voltage and finite-bias spectroscopy ($\partial G/\partial V_{sd}$), supplemented by analyzing superconducting-to-normal transition currents ($I_{sw}$).
model_or_system: The system is a gate-defined QPC realized in bilayer graphene (BLG) proximitized by an aluminum superconductor, allowing study of Andreev reflection and proximity effects.
key_observables: Enhanced conductance plateaus (Andreev enhancement), superconducting gap ($\Delta$), above-gap conductance anomaly (dip marking superconductivity loss), excess current ($I_{exc}$), and switching current ($I_{sw}$).
important_parameters: Low temperatures ($T=10 	ext{ mK}$), gate voltage ($V_{	ext{CG}}$) controlling mode quantization, and source-drain bias voltage ($V_{	ext{sd}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the superconducting gap features are robust indicators of proximity effects, and $I_{exc}$ is extracted by careful subtraction to minimize extrapolation errors.
figures_summary: Figures show quantized normal state conductance plateaus; finite-bias spectroscopy reveals coherence peaks at $\pm\Delta/e$ and an anomalous dip above the gap; switching current measurements demonstrate stepwise transitions correlated with QPC mode opening.
paper_structure: The paper systematically measures transport properties across different regimes: first establishing ballistic quantization, then observing Andreev enhancement in equilibrium, followed by characterizing the non-equilibrium collapse of superconductivity via conductance anomalies and quantized switching currents.
why_interesting: This work provides a clean experimental realization where fundamental quantum confinement (1D modes) dictates both the ground state superconducting properties (Andreev reflection) and the dynamic breakdown mechanisms, which is highly relevant for understanding mesoscopic superconducting circuits.
